forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Burnley forecasts £52k overspend for 2026/27 at quarter 2, down from £176k at quarter 1
news_drafts.lead:
Burnley Borough Council forecasts a net overspend of £52k for 2026/27 at the second quarter, down from a projected £176k at the first quarter. The revenue monitoring report for the Scrutiny Committee meeting on 18 November expects the position to break even by the end of the year.

The report says the second-quarter forecast includes identified salary savings as a contribution to the annual efficiency target, and that forecasts remain under review. Green Spaces and Amenities is forecast to overspend by £193k net, against £175k at the first quarter. Income from cremations, burials and interments is forecast to be £150k short for the year. The report says that projection is unchanged from the first quarter and is based on year-to-date receipts and typical September to March levels. It also records £25k of higher fuel costs, £6k of lost rental income at the Queens Park lodge and a £12k loss from the ice cream concession.

In the capital programme, the Minor Adaptations service had spent £81,389, 67% of its revised budget of £120,607, at mid-year. The capital narrative says: "It is currently anticipated there will be an overspend." The service is liaising with Lancashire County Council about it.

news_drafts.headline: Burnley lifts capital spending to £31m as debt falls and treasury returns beat forecast
news_drafts.lead: Burnley Council revised its capital spending upward by £6.2m to £31m in the first quarter of 2026–27, an 82 per cent increase on the previous year, but financed most of the rise through grants and reserves rather than new borrowing. The council's underlying borrowing need, known as its capital financing requirement, fell by £2.3m to £88.1m despite the higher spending, and its external debt decreased by £234k as scheduled repayments came due. Investment returns and debt management outperformed budget by £120k in the quarter. The council forecasts capital spending will fall sharply to £13.6m next year, suggesting the present level is a peak in a frontloaded programme. Financing costs are forecast to reach 24–28 per cent of the council's net revenue stream, nearly double the 14.7 per cent recorded in 2025–26, reflecting both elevated capital investment and the impact of higher interest rates on debt service.

news_drafts.headline: Burnley received "Reasonable Assurance" audit opinion for 2025/26 but Charter Walk acquisition had comprehensive controls
news_drafts.lead: Burnley's internal audit concluded that the council has a good system of controls but minor weaknesses in design or consistency of application may put the achievement of some objectives at risk. The council received a "Reasonable Assurance" overall audit opinion for 2025/26, the second-highest rating available. However, when auditors reviewed the council's acquisition of Charter Walk shopping centre in Burnley town centre — a decision presenting wide-ranging commercial risks — they found the risks were properly identified, controlled and continue to be monitored, and members were fully briefed before the decision. Internal audit gave comprehensive assurance that controls were sound and consistently applied, with no remedial actions required. The council implemented 100 per cent of high-priority audit recommendations against its 100 per cent target, though some lower-priority recommendations have been delayed.

findings.paper_title: Cap Bud Mon App 2 Capital Financing Qtr 2 2627 v3
findings.headline: Prairie Sports Village 3G Pitches (NEW) is listed with a revised budget of £825,000, one of several schemes marked NEW in the Green Spaces section.
findings.detail: The table marks several Green Spaces schemes as NEW, including Padel Tennis Courts, the Rakehead Recreation Ground Improvements and the Thompson Park Retaining Wall. The Padel Tennis Courts line shows no revised budget.
findings.matters: A council adding new schemes to its capital programme during the year is a sign of changing spending priorities, and other councils can compare which projects they are taking on.
findings.figures: £825,000 revised budget for Prairie Sports Village 3G Pitches (NEW)

findings.paper_title: Cap Bud Mon App 2 Capital Financing Qtr 2 2627 v3
findings.headline: The Waste Transfer Station/Depot Relocation has a revised budget of £3,026,093, with £2,428,000 in the first funding column and £598,093 in the second.
findings.detail: This is the largest single scheme in the Streetscene section, which has a total revised budget of £6,304,847. The table does not say which funding sources the two columns represent beyond their headings.
findings.matters: A depot relocation of this size is a major commitment, and its split between two funding sources shows how a council is paying for a single large asset.
findings.figures: £3,026,093 revised budget; £2,428,000 and £598,093 in the first two funding columns; Streetscene section total £6,304,847

findings.paper_title: Cap Bud Mon App 2 Capital Financing Qtr 2 2627 v3
findings.headline: The Better Care Grant line is £3,378,236 in the Housing & Development section, funded entirely from the Better Care Grant.
findings.detail: The scheme is shown as fully grant-funded, with no contribution from borrowing or reserves. It is the largest single grant-funded line in the Housing & Development section.
findings.matters: A large grant-funded housing line that carries no borrowing shows how much of the programme depends on external grant rather than the council's own balance sheet.
findings.figures: £3,378,236 revised budget, all from the Better Care Grant column

findings.paper_title: Cap Bud Mon App 2 Capital Financing Qtr 2 2627 v3
findings.headline: The Empty Homes Programme has a revised budget of £1,800,000, shown in the Housing & Development section.
findings.detail: The full £1,800,000 sits in the funding column headed Vacant Property Initiative Receipts, so the scheme is shown as wholly financed from that source. The table does not describe the programme's spending profile.
findings.matters: Using receipts from empty-property disposals to fund a housing programme is a funding choice other councils with similar stock could compare.

findings.paper_title: Cap Bud Mon App 2 Capital Financing Qtr 2 2627 v3
findings.headline: The 2026/27 capital programme totals £27,803,717 revised budget across five service areas, financed from a mix of revenue or reserves, prudential borrowing, grants and external funding.
findings.detail: The table covers Green Spaces & Amenities, Streetscene, Economy & Growth, Finance & Property, and Housing & Development. Each scheme's revised budget is split across the funding sources printed in the column headings.
findings.matters: A finance director, here or at another council, can use the size of the programme and its funding split to compare how much capital is being met from borrowing versus reserves, grants and receipts.
